what_it_does: Compute-in-memory (CIM) is a design strategy where arithmetic is done inside the memory chip itself rather than shipping data to a separate processor — this saves energy by avoiding constant data movement. Digital CIM chips store AI model weights in standard SRAM cells (fast, volatile memory made of six transistors per bit) and perform multiply-accumulate operations (the 'multiply many pairs of numbers then add the results' step that dominates AI workloads) by reading many rows of the memory array simultaneously. Running the chip at lower voltage saves energy, but it makes SRAM cells error-prone. Normal error-correcting codes (ECC — the same idea used in server memory to catch and fix occasional bit errors) work by reading one row at a time and checking a mathematical 'checksum'; they break down when you read and combine many rows simultaneously, which is exactly what digital CIM does. ER-DCIM introduces a different error-detection scheme based on residue codes — a technique where you track a compact mathematical fingerprint of the accumulated result — that can detect and correct errors in the combined output of many rows at once. It also incrementally repairs the underlying faulty SRAM cells in the background, and repurposes its error-resilience circuitry as a performance booster when the chip runs at full voltage, so no chip area is wasted.
